name: Barbados Museum and Historical Society
funding: Annual Government of Barbados grant, plus memberships, gate takings, shop sales, ground rentals and consulting fees. The government appoints five of its 14 council members.
watch: Incorporated in 1933 and opened in 1934 in a former British military prison at the Garrison, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
records_note: Posts annual reports 1994 to 2014 with audited financial statements, names its council and lists partners; nothing newer than 2014.

name: Barbican Art Gallery & The Curve
funding: £55M operating budget. Funded directly by the City of London Corporation as founder and principal funder, alongside Arts Council England and ticket revenues.
watch: Governed as a public civic corporation. The Curve gallery is permanently free to the public and hosts site-specific commissions.

name: Bemis Center
funding: Sponsor page, $20,000+ tier: Mellon, Art Bridges, NEA, Nebraska Arts Council, Sherwood, Holland, Heider and Hubbard foundations, Douglas County, National Indemnity, Omaha Steaks. 2024 expenses $2.4M.
watch: Non-profit artist residency and contemporary gallery in Omaha.
records_note: No annual reports found; 990s are on ProPublica, the sponsorship page names donors by tier without a date, and the board is listed.

name: Benesse Art Site Naoshima
funding: Built by the Benesse Foundation, funded by Benesse Corporation (Fukutake family). EFU Investments and a BPEA EQT fund bought 70.1% of Benesse in March 2024.
watch: Cultural revitalization initiative across Naoshima, Teshima, and Inujima founded by Soichiro Fukutake.
records_note: The Fukutake Foundation, which runs the art, lists yearly plans and reports from FY2007 and a dated board; no donor list is published.

name: Bergen Kunsthall
funding: Ministry of Culture, City of Bergen, Vestland county, Arts Council Norway, Fritt Ord, Sparebanken Norge, Nordic Council of Ministers, Bergesen Foundation, Westfal-Larsen fund and EGD Holding.
records_note: Its About page names 21 supporters and the 2026 board; accounts for 2023 to 2025 sit in the Norwegian register, with no annual report.

name: Bienal de Artes Mediales de Santiago
funding: Chile's Ministry of Cultures, through its collaborating-organisations programme and audiovisual fund, plus donations under the Cultural Donations Law. 2025 partners: SURA, Nescafé, La Tercera, Radio 13c.
watch: Run since 1993 by the Corporación Chilena de Video y Artes Electrónicas. The 17th edition ran 9 to 26 October 2025, centred on the GAM.
records_note: Its organiser CChV posts annual reports for 2018 to 2025, yearly balance sheets, a statement of its two public funding programmes, and its directorate.

name: Bienal de Cuenca
funding: Run by the Fundación Municipal Bienal de Cuenca, a city body. The 17th edition cost about $1.2M, from municipal money, private-company agreements and self-raised funds.
watch: In November 2025 a private group, DPOT, threatened the biennial over one work. It filed a complaint and kept the work on view.
records_note: Posts one annual report, for 2023, naming its agreement partners and the $163,913 raised; no accounts, board or standing sponsor page found.

name: Biennale Jogja
funding: Organised by Yayasan Biennale Yogyakarta, a state-funded foundation created in 2010. The Yogyakarta regional government ran the 2019 edition.
watch: On 9 October 2026 it announced closure after 16 years, citing rising censorship and violence against activists. It names no incident against itself.
records_note: Lists its patron board and executive but dated 2015; no annual reports, accounts or funder names are published.

name: Blak Dot Gallery
funding: Very small First Nations artist-run space; Australian Government Indigenous Languages and Arts, Creative Victoria and Merri-bek Council.
watch: First Nations-led gallery in Brunswick, founded in 2011. Hosted the 2014 '18C' protest show against Racial Discrimination Act changes.
records_note: ACNC holds financial reports for 2021 to 2026; the about page names three government funders, undated; no annual reports and no named board.

name: Bonnefanten
funding: Province of Limburg, the culture ministry and VriendenLoterij give structural support. Mondriaan Fund, Ammodo and others add project money. Over 150,000 visitors a year.
watch: Provincial public art museum governed under Dutch cultural sector transparency regulations.
records_note: Bonnefanten's ANBI page posts annual reports with accounts for 2017 to 2025 and names its supervisory board; the 2025 report names its funders.

name: Borusan Contemporary
funding: Corporate museum of Borusan Holding, run by the Borusan Kocabıyık Foundation in the holding's headquarters. Group units: EnBW wind power, steel pipe, Caterpillar dealing, car sales.
watch: Opened in 2011 during the 12th Istanbul Biennial. Borusan EnBW Enerji runs 725 MW of renewable plants.
records_note: Names its Board of Trustees and staff; no annual reports, accounts or funder list are published, and its listed partners are service vendors.

name: Botswana National Museum and Art Gallery
funding: Statutory museum set up by Act of Parliament in 1967 and run by the Department of National Museum and Monuments. Government funded its P33 million refurbishment, begun in 2020.
watch: Includes the National Art Gallery and the Octagon Gallery. Opened to the public in 1968.
records_note: Its official site is down and no ministry report could be opened, so reports, accounts, funders and board could not be checked.
